title: in and not in test whether a value belongs to a container
body: A membership test checks whether the value on the left belongs to the container on the right. In Python, in produces the membership result and not in produces its inverse.
detail: For lists, tuples, and sets, membership checks for an element. For strings it checks for a substring. For dictionaries, in checks keys rather than values. When reading the code, identify the container on the right first and then the value being searched for.
examples: "admin" in roles checks whether roles contains "admin".
"id" not in row checks whether the dictionary row lacks the key "id".

title: A slice selects a range from start up to but not including stop
body: The sequence[start:stop:step] form selects a range of values from a sequence. The element at stop is not included.
detail: Omitting start means starting from the beginning, omitting stop means continuing to the end, and omitting step uses a step of one. Negative indices can count from the end. Read start, stop, and step separately and write down the actual positions selected.
examples: items[:3] selects the first three elements.
text[1:5:2] selects every second position from index 1 up to but not including 5.

title: and, or, and not build conditions from truthy and falsy values
body: not reverses a truth value. and and or evaluate from left to right and short-circuit when the result is already determined.
detail: and and or do not necessarily return bool. x and y returns x when x is falsy; otherwise it evaluates and returns y. x or y returns x when x is truthy; otherwise it evaluates and returns y. Track both truthiness and the point where evaluation stops.
examples: ready and valid does not evaluate valid when ready is falsy.
name or 'guest' uses 'guest' when name is falsy.

title: A FastAPI application wires routers, dependencies, and middleware together
body: The app object created by FastAPI() is the central object that connects path operations, APIRouter objects, dependencies, middleware, and other application components.
detail: include_router() incorporates routes from an APIRouter into the main app. Depends resolves required dependencies for requests. Middleware wraps common request and response processing, while static/frontend configuration serves static assets. Options such as status_code declare path-operation response behavior.
examples: app.include_router(users.router) includes the routes from users.router.
Depends(get_current_user) connects user lookup as a request dependency.

title: Arithmetic operators combine operands to produce a calculated value
body: Operators such as +, -, *, /, //, %, and ** evaluate their operands and produce a result.
detail: Multiplication and division operators bind before addition and subtraction unless parentheses change the order. / performs division, // performs floor division, % gives the remainder, and ** performs exponentiation. Break long expressions into intermediate calculations when reading them.
examples: correct / total divides correct by total.
index % len(items) can keep an index within a repeating list range.

title: A keyword argument names the parameter that receives a value
body: The func(name=value) form passes a value by parameter name instead of relying only on position.
detail: Distinguish positional arguments from keyword arguments. Explicit names such as timeout=10 or axis=1 make the role of a value visible in the call. Parameters after * in a function definition may be keyword-only.
examples: requests.get(url, timeout=10) passes timeout as a keyword argument.
values.mean(axis=1) names the axis parameter explicitly.

title: * and ** collect multiple values or expand them again
body: In function definitions, *args and **kwargs collect arguments. In calls and collection displays, *iterable and **mapping expand multiple values.
detail: *args collects remaining positional arguments into a tuple and **kwargs collects keyword arguments into a dictionary. Conversely, func(*values) expands an iterable as positional arguments and func(**options) expands a mapping as keyword arguments. Assignment such as a, b = pair also unpacks iterable values into multiple targets.
examples: command = ['pip', 'install', *packages] expands packages into the list.
model.generate(**inputs) expands the inputs dictionary into keyword arguments.

title: A conditional expression selects exactly one of two values
body: x if condition else y evaluates condition first, then evaluates and returns x when true or y when false.
detail: Unlike a normal if statement, the conditional expression itself produces a value. The unselected expression is not evaluated. Read the middle condition first, then identify the value for each outcome.
examples: label = 'pass' if score >= 60 else 'retry'
value = cached if cached is not None else default

title: lambda creates a small function object from one expression
body: lambda parameters: expression creates an anonymous function object.
detail: The right side of lambda is one expression and its result becomes the return value. Lambdas are often used for short key functions passed to sorted or map. More complex logic is usually easier to read as a normal def.
examples: sorted(rows, key=lambda row: row['score']) sorts using score as the key.
lambda x: x * 2 creates a function that returns twice x.

title: NumPy code becomes easier to read when you start with shape and axis
body: NumPy array code often combines element-wise operations, broadcasting, reductions along an axis, and locating maximum values.
detail: Broadcasting compares shapes from the trailing dimensions and allows dimensions that are equal or where one side is 1. mean(axis=...) reduces values along the selected axis, while argmax(axis=...) returns the index of a maximum along that axis. Do not confuse the maximum value with its index.
examples: np.mean(a, axis=0) computes means along axis 0.
np.argmax(scores, axis=1) returns the column index of the largest value in each row.

title: A list comprehension collects repeated transformations into a new list
body: [expr for item in iterable if condition] iterates over an iterable, optionally filters items, and places the expression result in a new list.
detail: A useful reading order is to find the for clause first, identify the current item and source iterable, check any if filter, and finally read the expression at the front to see what is added to the result.
examples: [x * 2 for x in values] creates a new list of doubled values.
[row['id'] for row in rows if row['active']] collects IDs from active rows.

title: Path.glob and rglob find paths that match a pattern
body: Path.glob(pattern) iterates over matching paths relative to a Path, while Path.rglob(pattern) searches recursively through subdirectories.
detail: Conceptually, rglob(pattern) is similar to glob('**/' + pattern). Result ordering is not guaranteed, so sort the results when deterministic order matters. A ** pattern may traverse a large directory tree.
examples: Path('.').glob('*.json') finds matching JSON paths in the current directory.
Path('.').rglob('*.py') searches recursively for Python files.

title: @decorator applies another callable when a function or class is defined
body: A decorator passes the newly defined function or class object to another callable and binds the returned object back to the original name.
detail: When a def has @decorator above it, read it as creating the original function and then applying the decorator. Frameworks such as FastAPI also use decorators such as @app.get(...) to register functions as route handlers.
examples: @app.get('/health') registers the following function as the GET /health path operation.
A function under @wrapper is processed by wrapper when it is defined.

title: A dict comprehension collects repeated results as key:value pairs
body: {key_expr: value_expr for item in iterable if condition} creates a new dictionary from repeated key and value expressions.
detail: It is similar to a list comprehension but begins with separate key and value expressions. Identify the item in the for clause, check any filter, and then determine which key and value are produced. If the same key is produced again, the later assignment becomes the dictionary value for that key.
examples: {row['id']: row for row in rows} creates an ID lookup dictionary.
{x: x*x for x in range(3)} maps each number to its square.

title: An f-string inserts evaluated expressions into a string
body: Inside a string prefixed with f or F, each {expression} is evaluated at runtime and its result is inserted into the string.
detail: A replacement field can contain an expression. A colon introduces a format specifier such as numeric precision, and doubled braces {{ and }} represent literal braces.
examples: f'{name}: {score}' inserts the values of name and score.
f'{ratio:.2f}' formats ratio with two digits after the decimal point.

title: A function containing yield produces values one at a time
body: A function body containing yield defines a generator function, and calling that function returns a generator object.
detail: During iteration, execution runs until yield produces a value, pauses while preserving state, and resumes after that yield when another value is requested. This supports sequential processing without first constructing every result in a list.
examples: A function with yield 1 followed by yield 2 produces 1 and then 2 during iteration.
for chunk in generate_chunks(): consumes chunks as the generator yields them.

title: datetime.now creates a current datetime and isoformat turns it into text
body: datetime.now() creates a datetime containing the current date and time, and isoformat() produces its ISO-style string representation.
detail: Without a timezone argument, datetime.now() produces a local naive datetime. Logs and stored data should therefore use an explicit timezone policy when that distinction matters. isoformat(timespec=...) can control the displayed precision.
examples: datetime.now().isoformat() can record the current time as text.
datetime.now().isoformat(timespec='seconds') formats the value through seconds.

title: rollback cancels changes in a transaction that has not been committed
body: In a database transaction, commit confirms pending changes while rollback cancels the current pending transaction changes.
detail: Grouping related writes in one transaction prevents only part of a multi-step operation from remaining after a failure. sqlite3 Connection.rollback() has nothing to undo when no transaction is open. Check where commit and rollback occur on success and exception paths.
examples: On an exception during database writes, connection.rollback() can cancel pending changes.
After all operations succeed, connection.commit() confirms them.

title: AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained loads a tokenizer that matches a model
body: Hugging Face AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id_or_path) inspects a model ID or local path and loads the corresponding pretrained tokenizer implementation.
detail: A tokenizer converts text into token IDs understood by a model and can decode model output back to text. Reading the model repository ID or local path tells you which tokenizer assets are being loaded.
examples: AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained('bert-base-uncased') loads the tokenizer for that model.
tokenizer(text) converts text into model inputs such as token IDs.

title: islice selects positions from an iterator without first building a sequence
body: itertools.islice(iterable, start, stop, step) returns an iterator over selected elements using slice-like positions.
detail: It can consume just the required part of an iterable instead of converting everything to a list first. start, stop, and step cannot be negative. With stop=None, iteration can continue until the input is exhausted.
examples: islice(stream, 10) yields the first ten items from stream.
islice(values, 2, 8, 2) yields every second item from index 2 up to but not including 8.

title: list.index returns the index of the first equal value
body: list.index(value) returns the zero-based index of the first list element equal to value.
detail: When the value is absent, list.index raises ValueError rather than returning -1. Optional start and stop arguments limit the search region, but the returned index is still relative to the full list.
examples: ['a', 'b', 'a'].index('a') returns 0.
If target may be absent, account for the possible ValueError from items.index(target).

title: A # comment is explanatory source text rather than executed code
body: In Python source, a # outside a string starts a comment that continues to the end of the physical line and is ignored by the syntax.
detail: Comments are useful for explaining intent or constraints, but they should not be read as executable statements. A # character inside a string literal is ordinary character data.
examples: In total += value  # running total, the text after # is not executed.
In text = "#tag", the # is inside a string and is data.

title: is asks whether two references identify the same object; == compares values
body: is and is not test object identity, while == and != test equality according to the values' comparison behavior.
detail: Two different objects can contain equal values, so is and == are not interchangeable. Testing a singleton such as None commonly uses x is None.
examples: value is None tests whether value is the None object.
a == b compares whether a and b are equal in value.

title: NameError means Python could not find a binding for a name
body: NameError occurs when Python evaluates a name but cannot find a corresponding value in an accessible scope.
detail: Check misspelled variable names, names used before definition, missing imports, and local names referenced outside their scope. Trace the failing name back to where it should have been bound.
examples: print(total) can raise NameError when total has never been defined.
Using a module name without importing or defining it can fail name lookup.

title: A type annotation records the intended type of a variable, parameter, or return value
body: Syntax such as x: int or def f(x: int) -> str attaches type information to names, parameters, or return values.
detail: Annotations help IDEs and static analysis tools understand code, but they do not by themselves mean that Python automatically converts or validates every runtime value. In x: int = 3, the annotation and the actual assignment are separate aspects of the statement.
examples: count: int = 0 records an int annotation and assigns 0.
def load(path: str) -> dict: annotates the parameter and intended return type.

title: random.seed initializes the state of the pseudo-random generator
body: random.seed(value) initializes the pseudo-random number generator used by the random module.
detail: Reusing a seed can help reproduce the same pseudo-random sequence for tests or experiments when the call sequence is also controlled. The random module is not intended for cryptographic secret generation.
examples: random.seed(42) helps reproduce a later sequence of random calls.
For experiment comparison, keep both the seed and the order of random calls controlled.

title: requestAnimationFrame schedules an animation callback before the next repaint
body: window.requestAnimationFrame(callback) asks the browser to invoke callback before the next repaint.
detail: Each request schedules one callback, so continuous animation normally requests another frame from inside the callback. Using the callback timestamp allows animation progress to be based on elapsed time instead of assuming a fixed display refresh rate.
examples: requestAnimationFrame(render) schedules render for the next repaint.
A continuous animation calls requestAnimationFrame(render) again from render.

title: subprocess.run executes an external command and returns its completion result
body: subprocess.run(args, ...) starts an external command, waits for it to complete, and returns a CompletedProcess object.
detail: Passing args as a list clearly separates the executable from its arguments. With check=True a non-zero exit status can raise CalledProcessError, while capture_output=True can capture stdout and stderr.
examples: subprocess.run(['python', '--version'], check=True) checks whether the command succeeds.
result.returncode gives the external process exit code.

title: tqdm wraps an iterable while displaying its progress
body: tqdm(iterable) yields the same items as the original iterable while dynamically displaying iteration progress.
detail: When the iterable length is available, tqdm can infer the total. For manually managed work, total can be supplied and update() can advance the counter. The wrapper reports progress; it does not transform the underlying values.
examples: for row in tqdm(rows): iterates through rows while showing a progress bar.
tqdm(total=filesize) with update(n) can track manually reported progress.
